transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, thank you. It’s... it’s a bit hard to talk about, honestly. I suppose what finally made me say something is that... well, you see, the shop has been incredibly busy lately. I’m a dispensing optician, and we just got this new line of frames in, and the hinges on them are absolutely dreadful. I spent half of yesterday just trying to adjust a pair of varifocals for this lovely older gentleman, but it really takes it out of you, you know? By the time I get home, I’m just completely drained. 

But anyway, what brings me in is that... after I eat too much in the evenings, I’ve been going upstairs and making myself throw up. And then I just come back down and act as if I’m just tidying the kitchen or getting ready for bed. My husband hasn't a clue, really. He's usually just glued to the television watching those World War II documentaries—he's absolutely fascinated by Churchill, though I've always found all that history stuff a bit dry myself... but yes, that's what's been happening.
How often do you find yourself eating a large amount of food in one sitting, and do you feel a loss of control during these episodes?

Well, it's... it's quite often, really. When I'm alone in the kitchen, I just... I can't seem to stop myself. Like just the other evening, after I’d made a lovely shepherd’s pie—my husband’s favorite, you know, though he always complains if I don't get the mash perfectly crisp on top. He says his mother used to use a fork to make little peaks, which is just so fussy if you ask me. But anyway, when he was in the sitting room, I just went through the rest of the pie, and then I found myself eating half a block of cheddar, a sleeve of water biscuits, and almost all the lemon drizzle cake I’d baked for my book club. 

We're reading that new historical fiction novel everyone's talking about, though honestly, I prefer a good mystery. Agatha Christie, that sort of thing. But yes, I just eat and eat, far more than I’d ever put on a plate for a proper meal. It's like I'm completely on autopilot and I just can't rein it in once I start. It's really quite embarrassing.
How often do you make yourself vomit after these episodes of overeating?

Well, since last winter, really. There has hardly been a single week when I haven’t had at least one of those... private eating spells, I suppose you could call them. And then I try to make up for it by throwing up, or skipping my breakfast the next day, or just walking for miles. 

I actually started walking more because my sister bought me one of those fancy step-counter watches for my birthday. She’s always been the athletic one in the family, you know. Played tennis at university, still plays every Tuesday morning at her local club. She keeps telling me I should join her, but honestly, the outfits they wear... and I just don't have the hand-eye coordination for it. Plus, with my work at the opticians, I spend all day dealing with people’s vision, the last thing I want is a tennis ball flying at my head! We did try badminton once on a family holiday to Cornwall—oh, it must have been about ten years ago now. It rained the entire time, absolutely poured, so we were stuck indoors in this drafty little sports hall... but yes, since winter, it's been at least once a week.

When you have these episodes of eating large amounts of food, do they happen even when you’re not feeling like you need to make up for it later, or do you usually feel like you need to do something like throw up or walk a lot after?

Well, I always feel like I have to do *something* after, yes. It's never just... eating and then moving on with the evening. I always have to fix it, you know? Throwing up, or like I said, the walking. 

I actually wore a hole right through the sole of my good walking boots last month. The brown leather ones, they were so comfortable. I took them to that little cobbler on High Street—you know, the one next to the bakery that does those wonderful sourdough loaves? Though I don't buy bread there anymore, obviously. But the cobbler, he said they were beyond repair. He’s such a lovely man, always has a story about his time in the merchant navy. He told me once about a storm off the coast of South America that lasted for three days. Can you imagine? Just rocking back and forth on the ocean like that. I get seasick just taking the ferry over to France. My husband loves it, of course. He’ll stand out on the deck in the freezing cold just to watch the waves... but yes, I always feel like I have to make up for the eating. Every single time.
